# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review of Diagnostic and Therapeutic Advances

### Introduction
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a progressive and historically underdiagnosed restrictive cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of insoluble, misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardial interstitium [1,2]. While more than 30 proteins can form amyloid, systemic light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis account for over 95% of clinical cases [3,4]. In AL amyloidosis, a monoclonal plasma cell clone produces unstable immunoglobulin light chains that aggregate into amyloid fibrils [4]. Conversely, ATTR amyloidosis arises from the dissociation and misfolding of the liver-synthesized transthyretin tetramer [1]. ATTR is further classified into wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt), which occurs predominantly in older adults without genetic mutations, and hereditary or variant ATTR (ATTRv), caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the *TTR* gene [1,5]. Epidemiological data have demonstrated a rising prevalence of both forms, particularly ATTRwt in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [5,6]. Historically, CA was considered rare due to diagnostic delays; however, a heightened clinical index of suspicion is altering its perceived epidemiology [7,8].

### Clinical Presentation and Diagnostics
Patients with CA typically present with symptoms of heart failure, such as dyspnea, fatigue, and lower extremity edema [9]. Systemic "red flags" are crucial for early recognition [8]. In ATTR, these include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and spontaneous biceps tendon rupture, which can precede cardiac symptoms by years [1,6]. In AL amyloidosis, clinical cues such as periorbital purpura, macroglossia, and nephrotic-range proteinuria point toward a systemic plasma cell dyscrasia [3,10].

Electrocardiography frequently demonstrates a pseudoinfarction pattern or low voltage, which is highly suggestive when discordant with the degree of left ventricular hypertrophy on imaging [9,10]. Echocardiography is the initial imaging modality, classically revealing symmetric ventricular wall thickening, biatrial enlargement, and a restrictive diastolic filling pattern [10]. Speckle-tracking echocardiography showing relative "apical sparing" of longitudinal strain is a highly sensitive and specific hallmark of CA [11]. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides superior tissue characterization, demonstrating diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and marked expansion of the myocardial extracellular volume (ECV) fraction [12].

For patients suspected of having ATTR, technetium-99m labeled bone scintigraphy—using pyrophosphate (PYP) or 3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid (DPD)—has revolutionized the diagnostic paradigm [13,14]. When combined with the rigorous exclusion of a clonal plasma cell disorder, a Grade 2 or 3 myocardial uptake of these radiotracers has a nearly 100% specificity for ATTR, enabling a nonbiopsy diagnosis [15,16].

### Prognostication and Staging
Accurate prognostication is vital, particularly in AL amyloidosis where early mortality remains high [3,17]. Staging systems primarily utilize cardiac biomarkers, specifically N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) and cardiac troponins [17,18]. The revised Mayo Clinic staging system for AL amyloidosis incorporates NT-proBNP, troponin T, and the difference between involved and uninvolved serum free light chains (dFLC) to stratify risk [17]. Longitudinal monitoring of these biomarkers is also essential for assessing treatment response [19].

### Therapeutic Breakthroughs
The management of CA has undergone a dramatic transformation, shifting from purely supportive care to highly effective disease-modifying therapies [9]. In AL amyloidosis, the immediate therapeutic goal is rapid suppression of the clone producing the toxic light chain to facilitate organ recovery [3]. The landmark ANDROMEDA trial established the combination of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (CyBorD) as the standard of care, achieving unprecedented rates of hematologic complete response and major organ preservation [20].

For ATTR amyloidosis, therapeutic strategies target different steps of the amyloid cascade [1]. Transthyretin stabilizers bind to the thyroxine-binding sites, preventing the dissociation of the TTR tetramer into unstable monomeric subunits [1,21]. The landmark ATTR-ACT trial demonstrated that tafamidis significantly reduces all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations in patients with ATTR cardiomyopathy [21], building on initial efficacy established in familial polyneuropathy [22]. More recently, the novel stabilizer acoramidis achieved highly potent TTR stabilization, meeting its primary composite endpoint in the ATTRibute-CM trial and demonstrating significant clinical benefit [28].

Alternatively, gene-silencing therapies act upstream by inhibiting the hepatic synthesis of transthyretin [1]. In clinical trials of hereditary ATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy, the small interfering RNA (siRNA) patisiran [23] and the antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) inotersen [24] successfully halted neurological progression. The therapeutic indication was subsequently extended to cardiac disease; the APOLLO-B trial demonstrated that patisiran preserves functional capacity and quality of life in patients with ATTR cardiomyopathy [25]. Furthermore, vutrisiran, a next-generation subcutaneously administered siRNA, significantly reduced all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events in ATTR cardiomyopathy in the HELIOS-B trial [26]. The ligand-conjugated ASO eplontersen has also shown profound TTR suppression and clinical benefit in variant ATTR polyneuropathy [27], representing another major milestone in this rapidly evolving pharmacotherapy landscape.

### Consensus and Multidisciplinary Care
Given the multisystem nature of amyloidosis and the rapid evolution of therapeutics, both the American Heart Association (AHA) and the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) emphasize the necessity of multidisciplinary amyloidosis centers [29,30]. Collaborations between cardiologists, hematologists, neurologists, and nephrologists are essential to optimize early diagnosis, initiate targeted therapies, and manage complications such as arrhythmias and heart failure symptoms [29,30].

### Conclusion
Cardiac amyloidosis has evolved from a fatal, untreatable condition to a highly manageable disease. Advances in noninvasive imaging have streamlined the diagnostic pathway, while innovative therapies targeting both the plasma cell clone in AL and the TTR pathway in ATTR have fundamentally altered the disease course, vastly improving patient survival and quality of life.
